note: You are reading the image plan for a game — a list of image-generation prompts. Each entry names an asset (a full-screen background/setting, a character sprite, an optional hero title image, an optional climax illustration) and carries a `description` that is the ENTIRE text handed to an image generator: the generator sees nothing else, so each description must produce a concrete, on-style image on its own. Backgrounds are the game's settings; character entries are the cast's sprites; a title image reads the premise at a glance; a CG marks a story high point. Judge only the prompts on the page — whether each would render the intended image and whether the set holds one coherent look. For each criterion pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches, and quote specific descriptions as evidence.

criteria.name: visual_specificity
criteria._authoring: The core of the whole artifact and the easiest to wave through: a prompt built from mood words ('dark, atmospheric, dramatic') is grammatical and evocative but renders generic mush, because the generator has no concrete content to place. Anchored to the observed vague-prompt attractor. GATE: below level 2 this caps the overall at its own score — a plan of mood-summary prompts cannot post a decent number on the strength of its style notes or its coverage, because none of it renders as intended.
criteria.description: Does each description specify a concrete, renderable image — naming actual objects, their arrangement in the frame, and a specific quality of light — rather than summarizing a mood? A usable prompt says what is IN the picture; a vague one only says how it should feel.

levels.0: Mood summaries. Descriptions are built from atmosphere words — 'a dark hallway, mysterious, dramatic lighting' — naming no specific objects or composition. The generator has nothing concrete to render; any two prompts of the same type would produce interchangeable images.
levels.1: Barely concrete. A description names its subject and little else ('a foggy dock at night'), leaving out the objects, arrangement, and specific light that would make the image particular; several prompts are still mostly mood words.
levels.2: Concrete but thin. Each prompt names its subject and a couple of real objects, enough to render something recognizable, but framing and light are generic and the image would look like stock art of that place rather than this game's.
levels.3: Specific. Most descriptions name the objects present, roughly where they sit in the frame, and a particular quality of light — a reader can picture the shot, and it has at least one detail a generic image of the same place would lack.
levels.4: Fully realized. Every description reads as a composed shot — named contents, their spatial relationship, framing, and specific lighting — such that the generated image would be unmistakably this scene and no other, with no filler mood words doing the work.

criteria.name: background_environmental_discipline
criteria._authoring: Anchored to a proven real failure (quality backlog): the image model renders any creature, character, or person named in a BACKGROUND description AS the subject of the picture, so a backdrop that mentions 'a guard by the door' comes back as a portrait of a guard with no room. Backgrounds must stay purely environmental — inhabitants belong in sprite entries, and only the title/CG entries may name people. Scope this criterion to background entries only.
criteria.description: Do the background descriptions stay purely environmental — place, objects, architecture, and light, with no creature, character, or person named as content? A background exists to be a backdrop that sprites stand in front of; naming a living subject in it makes the generator render that subject instead of the room.

levels.0: Backgrounds are populated. Multiple background descriptions name a creature, character, or person as part of the scene, so those images would render as portraits of that subject rather than as an empty, usable backdrop.
levels.1: Frequently populated. More than one background slips in a person or animal, or leans on a figure to carry the composition, undermining its use as a backdrop.
levels.2: Mostly clean. Backgrounds are environmental with one lapse — a single description names an incidental figure that would intrude on the render.
levels.3: Environmental. Every background describes only place, objects, and light; inhabitants are left to the sprites, and any people appear only where they belong (a title or climax image).
levels.4: Disciplined and deliberate. Backgrounds are strictly environmental and composed as backdrops — space left where characters will stand, framing that reads as a set rather than a populated photo — with inhabitants cleanly confined to the sprite entries.

criteria.name: coverage
criteria._authoring: That every cast member has a sprite entry is close to mechanically enforced, so parity alone lands mid-scale; the top levels require the settings the story actually needs (not one room the whole game is forced into) plus the title and a climax illustration where the premise implies a peak.
criteria.description: Does the plan cover every asset the game will display — a distinct background for each physical setting the premise implies (not one room every scene is forced into), a sprite for each cast member, a hero title image, and a climax illustration where the story implies a high point?

levels.0: Major gaps. A whole class is missing or collapsed — no character sprites, or a single background where the premise clearly moves between settings, so most scenes would have no place to happen.
levels.1: Thin. Sprites roughly match the cast, but the settings are undercounted (distinct places share one backdrop) and there is no title image.
levels.2: Adequate. A sprite per cast member and a background per obvious setting, but the premise implies places or a climax that have no asset, or the title image is missing.
levels.3: Complete. Every setting the premise implies has its own background, every cast member has a sprite, and a title image is present; a clear story peak has a candidate illustration.
levels.4: Complete and judged. Coverage is exact — one background per distinct displayed setting with none redundant or missing, a sprite per character, a title image that reads the premise, and a climax illustration placed where the story actually peaks.

criteria.name: style_consistency
criteria._authoring: Two things at once: a single art direction folded INLINE into every prompt (the generator sees only the one description, so a bare 'foggy dock' with no style renders off-model), and characters that read as the same visual world yet distinct from each other.
criteria.description: Do all the prompts describe one coherent visual world — a single style, palette, and lighting approach carried inline through every description — and do the characters read as distinct people within that shared look rather than recolors of one base?

levels.0: Five sources. Prompts mix incompatible styles (flat anime beside photoreal), or most descriptions carry no style cue at all, so the generated set would not look like one game.
levels.1: Inconsistent. A style is stated somewhere but not carried into most descriptions, or the palette and lighting drift enough that assets would clash on screen.
levels.2: Loosely unified. A shared style is present in most prompts but applied unevenly; the set mostly hangs together, and characters are distinguishable but lean on a single base.
levels.3: Coherent. One style, palette, and lighting approach runs through nearly every description, and each character has distinct, grounded features so the cast reads as different people in the same world.
levels.4: One world. Every prompt commits the same art direction inline while varying composition and framing per image, and each character is unmistakably distinct yet clearly belongs to the same visual set — the assets would read as screenshots of a single game.
